title: When Is Muon Optimal? Radial Fragility and Minimax Geometry

paper.title: When Is Muon Optimal? Radial Fragility and Minimax Geometry
paper.abstract:
Abstract Muon replaces a matrix gradient by an approximate polar factor and has
shown strong empirical performance in neural-network training. The
Isotropic Curvature Model (ICM) provides a curvature-based explanation
for this update by asking when gradient orthogonalization minimizes a
one-step local-loss surrogate. We investigate the stability of this
explanation when the fixed input radius of the ICM is replaced by a
general radial law.
We introduce the Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model (RR-ICM) and
the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set, which encodes exact scaled-polar
optimality as a geometric condition on the positive polar factor of the
gradient. We derive an exact characterization of this set for arbitrary
radial laws and show that all nonscalar admissible responses arise from
radial atoms aligned with curvature kinks. Consequently, every atomless
radial law exhibits zero-capacity rigidity: exact scaled-polar
optimality is possible only when the gradient is already a scaled
column isometry.
To connect the curvature-based framework with the established spectral
geometry of Muon, we introduce the Minimax RR-ICM by replacing
directional averaging with worst-case optimization over probability
laws on the sphere. We prove that every nonzero global minimizer lies
on the polar ray of the gradient, while its scale is determined by a
one-dimensional convex problem. The corresponding admissibility
geometry is a positive-semidefinite trace slab, in sharp contrast to
the spherical-zonoid geometry of the RR-ICM. Together, these results
expose the radial fragility of average-curvature explanations and
provide a new minimax variational characterization of Muon’s polar
direction.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Muon is a matrix-aware optimizer designed primarily for hidden-layer weight matrices. Given a momentum-smoothed matrix gradient M t = U t ​ Σ t ​ V t ⊤ , M_{t}=U_{t}\Sigma_{t}V_{t}^{\top}, Muon applies a small number of Newton–Schulz iterations to approximate its polar factor U t ​ V t ⊤ U_{t}V_{t}^{\top} , while non-matrix parameters such as embeddings, normalization parameters, biases, and output heads are typically handled by AdamW [ 8 ] . Consequently, Muon preserves the left and right singular subspaces of the momentum update while largely flattening its nonzero singular values. In this sense, it replaces a potentially highly anisotropic matrix update by an approximately semi-orthogonal one. Muon first attracted attention through strong empirical performance in small-scale language-model and image-classification training, and was subsequently shown to scale to substantially larger language models. Liu et al. [ 14 ] identified weight decay and parameter-shape-dependent update scaling as key ingredients for stable large-scale training, and developed a memory- and communication-efficient distributed implementation. Their scaling-law experiments reported that Muon required approximately 52 % 52\% of the training FLOPs needed by a tuned AdamW baseline at matched performance. They further used Muon to train Moonlight, a 3 ​ B / 16 ​ B 3\mathrm{B}/16\mathrm{B} mixture-of-experts model, on 5.7 5.7 trillion tokens. These results suggest that matrix-gradient orthogonalization is not merely a small-model heuristic, but can provide meaningful optimization gains at the scale of modern language-model training. Figure 1 : Radial averaging is a small perturbation at the level of function values but a singular perturbation at a kink. For H ⁡ ( t ) = ( t − 1 ) + H(t)=(t-1)_{+} and R ε ∼ Unif ⁡ [ 1 − ε , 1 + ε ] R_{\varepsilon}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon] , the averaged profile H ε ​ ( t ) = 𝔼 ​ ( R ε ​ t − 1 ) + H_{\varepsilon}(t)=\mathbb{E}(R_{\varepsilon}t-1)_{+} differs from H H only within an O ⁡ ( ε ) O(\varepsilon) transition layer. Nevertheless, the interval ∂ H ⁡ ( 1 ) = [ 0 , 1 ] \partial H(1)=[0,1] is replaced by the unique derivative H ε ′ ​ ( 1 ) = 1 / 2 + ε / 4 H_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}(1)=1/2+\varepsilon/4 . Theoretical interest in this transformation extends beyond Muon itself. Earlier work on stochastic and preconditioned spectral descent already explored matrix updates adapted to spectral geometry [ 4 , 5 ] . More recent studies have interpreted Muon through several closely related viewpoints, including spectral-norm steepest descent and architecture-dependent duality maps [ 2 , 3 ] , norm-constrained linear minimization oracles [ 15 ] , non-Euclidean trust-region optimization [ 10 ] , and implicit spectral-norm constraints [ 6 ] . These perspectives establish why the polar factor is a natural or optimal update under a specified or implicitly induced spectral geometry. Related work has also connected Muon to matrix-aware preconditioning and structured curvature surrogates [ 12 , 7 ] . Su [ 20 ] took a complementary approach. Rather than prescribing a norm geometry, constraint set, or trust region, he derived the Isotropic Curvature Model (ICM) as a one-step variational surrogate for the local change in a neural-network training loss, under an isotropy assumption on its curvature across perturbation directions. Within this surrogate framework, he asked under what curvature conditions gradient orthogonalization—and, in particular, Muon’s polar update—emerges as an exact optimal matrix update. Given a gradient matrix G ∈ ℝ m × n G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , the ICM considers J sph ​ ( Q , G ) = − ⟨ G , Q ⟩ + 𝔼 ζ ​ H ​ ( ‖ Q ​ ζ ‖ 2 ) , ζ ∼ Unif ⁡ ( 𝕊 n − 1 ) , J_{\mathrm{sph}}(Q;G)=-\langle G,Q\rangle+\mathbb{E}_{\zeta}H(\|Q\zeta\|_{2}),\qquad\zeta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}), where H H is a scalar curvature profile. If G = P ​ S G=PS is the thin polar decomposition and Q = c ​ P Q=cP , then ‖ Q ​ ζ ‖ 2 = c \|Q\zeta\|_{2}=c for every ζ ∈ 𝕊 n − 1 \zeta\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} . Hence, when H H has a kink at c c , all spherical samples lie at the same nondifferentiable point. Direction-dependent subgradient selections may then generate a nonscalar matrix response capable of supporting a scaled polar update. The fixed-sphere assumption is often motivated by high-dimensional radial concentration [ 21 ] . For example, a standard Gaussian vector satisfies Z n = ρ n ​ ζ , Z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I n ) , ρ n = ‖ Z ‖ 2 n , \frac{Z}{\sqrt{n}}=\rho_{n}\zeta,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}),\qquad\rho_{n}=\frac{\|Z\|_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}, where ζ \zeta is uniform on 𝕊 n − 1 \mathbb{S}^{n-1} and independent of ρ n \rho_{n} , and ρ n → 1 \rho_{n}\to 1 in probability. For smooth observables, this suggests that the normalized-Gaussian and fixed-sphere models should be asymptotically close. Exact polar optimality in the ICM, however, relies on a set-valued subdifferential at a kink, and radial concentration need not preserve this first-order variational geometry. A deterministic radius can place every sample exactly on the kink, whereas an atomless random radius hits any prescribed kink with probability zero, no matter how concentrated its law is. Thus, a thin random shell and a fixed sphere may be arbitrarily close in radius while differing discontinuously in the subdifferential structure that governs exact optimality. Figure 1 illustrates this distinction for a scalar hinge: radial averaging changes function values only within a shrinking transition layer, yet replaces a set-valued subgradient by a unique smooth response. Motivated by the preceding observation, we introduce a natural extension of the ICM in which the input radius is allowed to vary while the directional component remains uniform on the sphere. We call this the Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model (RR-ICM): J R ​ ( Q , G ) = − ⟨ G , Q ⟩ + 𝔼 R , ζ ​ H ​ ( R ​ ‖ Q ​ ζ ‖ 2 ) , ζ ∼ Unif ⁡ ( 𝕊 n − 1 ) , R ⟂ ⟂ ζ . J_{R}(Q;G)=-\langle G,Q\rangle+\mathbb{E}_{R,\zeta}H(R\|Q\zeta\|_{2}),\qquad\zeta\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}),\qquad R\perp\!\!\!\perp\zeta. The model randomizes only the input radius while preserving rotational symmetry. This extension leads to our first structural question. Question 1: Exact polar optimality under radial variation When the fixed-sphere ICM is extended to a general radial law, under what conditions can a scaled polar factor c ​ P cP remain an exact global minimizer? Can these conditions be characterized completely in terms of the radial law, the curvature profile, and the spectrum of the gradient’s positive polar factor? To answer this question, we introduce the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set , which encodes exact scaled-polar optimality as a geometric condition on the positive polar factor of the gradient. For an arbitrary radial law, we prove the exact representation A ⁡ ( J R , c ​ P ) = b c ​ I n + w c ​ 𝒦 n , A(J_{R},cP)=b_{c}I_{n}+w_{c}\mathcal{K}_{n}, where 𝒦 n \mathcal{K}_{n} is a spherical zonoid and w c w_{c} records the total atom–kink resonance at scale c c . This formula gives a complete geometric characterization of the gradient spectra compatible with exact polar optimality. In particular, all nonscalar spectral freedom is generated by radial atoms aligned with curvature kinks; when the radial law is atomless, the admissibility set collapses to a single scalar matrix. This rigidity reveals a precise limitation of the average-curvature explanation. Although radial concentration may make a thin shell close to a sphere at the level of function values, exact polar optimality for a general nonscalar gradient spectrum depends on a fragile atom–kink resonance. Thus, the average RR-ICM alone does not provide a radially robust variational explanation of Muon’s polar update. This conclusion creates an explanatory tension. Muon’s polar direction has broad spectral-geometric interpretations and performs robustly across large-scale training settings [ 14 ] , whereas exact polar optimality in the average RR-ICM can be destroyed by an arbitrarily thin atomless radial perturbation. This leads to our second structural question. Question 2: A curvature-based bridge to spectral geometry Does there exist a natural counterpart of the RR-ICM that retains its local-curvature and random-radius structure, while selecting the polar factor as the optimal matrix direction for general gradient spectra? Can such a formulation establish a variational connection between the ICM viewpoint and the established spectral interpretations of Muon? To address this question, we replace the prescribed uniform directional law in the RR-ICM by a worst-case choice over all probability laws on the sphere. Writing 𝒫 ⁡ ( 𝕊 n − 1 ) \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}) for the set of Borel probability measures on 𝕊 n − 1 \mathbb{S}^{n-1} , we introduce the Minimax RR-ICM J R M ​ ( Q , G ) = − ⟨ G , Q ⟩ + sup ν ∈ 𝒫 ⁡ ( 𝕊 n − 1 ) 𝔼 ζ ∼ ν ​ H ¯ R ​ ( ‖ Q ​ ζ ‖ 2 ) . J_{R}^{\mathrm{M}}(Q;G)=-\langle G,Q\rangle+\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})}\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim\nu}\overline{H}_{R}(\|Q\zeta\|_{2}). We prove that, whenever the Minimax RR-ICM admits a nonzero global minimizer, every such minimizer lies on the polar ray generated by the gradient: its operator-norm-normalized matrix direction is exactly the polar factor of G G . The Minimax RR-ICM therefore provides a new curvature-based minimax variational characterization of Muon’s polar update. Moreover, because it is obtained from the RR-ICM by changing only how directional variation is aggregated, this characterization establishes a direct variational bridge between the ICM viewpoint and the established spectral-geometric interpretations of Muon.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our main contributions are summarized as follows. 1. A polar-factor admissibility framework. We introduce the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set , which reformulates exact optimality of a scaled polar update as a convex-set membership condition on the positive polar factor of the gradient. This provides a common variational language for comparing different curvature models. 2. Exact polar-factor admissibility in the RR-ICM. For the Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model, we characterize completely the gradient spectra compatible with exact scaled-polar optimality. For an arbitrary radial law, we prove A ⁡ ( J R , c ​ P ) = b c ​ I n + w c ​ 𝒦 n , A(J_{R},cP)=b_{c}I_{n}+w_{c}\mathcal{K}_{n}, where 𝒦 n \mathcal{K}_{n} is a spherical zonoid and w c w_{c} records the total atom–kink resonance at scale c c . This representation shows that radial atoms aligned with curvature kinks are the sole source of nonscalar admissible responses, and yields a spectral-capacity bound and an exact rigidity result for atomless radial laws. 3. A new minimax variational characterization of Muon. We introduce the Minimax RR-ICM by replacing directional averaging with worst-case optimization over spherical probability laws. We prove that every nonzero global minimizer lies on the polar ray of the gradient, while its scale is determined by an exact one-dimensional convex optimization problem. 4. A geometric bridge between curvature and spectral interpretations. We characterize the Minimax Polar-Factor Admissibility Set as a positive-semidefinite trace slab and place it in direct comparison with the spherical-zonoid geometry of the average RR-ICM. The two models thereby reveal distinct mechanisms of polar optimality: atom–kink resonance under directional averaging and operator-norm subdifferential geometry under directional minimax robustification.

sections.heading: Organization.
sections.text: Section 2 formulates the RR-ICM and isolates the effect of radial randomness through an effective curvature profile. Section 3 gives the exact characterization of the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set and derives the resulting spectral-capacity and atomless-rigidity consequences. Section 4 introduces the Minimax RR-ICM, establishes its polar optimizer geometry, and compares its admissibility set with that of the average RR-ICM. The proofs are collected in Section 5 , and Section 6 concludes with a discussion of the scope, interpretation, and limitations of the framework.

sections.heading: 2 The Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model
sections.text: Because the Gaussian radius concentrates around one in high dimensions, the fixed-sphere and normalized-Gaussian models become close at the level of ordinary function values. This section explains why that closeness need not preserve first-order variational structure at a kink, and then formulates the random-radius extension of the ICM.

sections.heading: 3 Characterization of the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set
sections.text: This section gives a complete geometric characterization of exact scaled-polar optimality in the RR-ICM. We first recast Su’s fixed-sphere optimality condition in terms of the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set, which records the positive polar factors compatible with a scaled polar minimizer. We then characterize this set exactly under an arbitrary radial law as a translated and dilated spherical zonoid. The resulting formula identifies atom–kink resonance as the sole source of nonscalar admissible responses and leads to a quantitative spectral-capacity bound. As a sharp consequence, every atomless radial law exhibits zero-capacity rigidity: exact scaled-polar optimality can occur only when the gradient’s positive polar factor is scalar.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: This paper studied the variational status of Muon’s polar direction within curvature-based one-step models. Starting from the Isotropic Curvature Model, we asked whether its fixed-sphere explanation of gradient orthogonalization remains valid when the input radius is allowed to vary. The resulting analysis reveals a sharp distinction between radial concentration at the level of function values and stability of the first-order geometry governing exact optimality. To make this distinction precise, we introduced the Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model and the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set. The latter converts exact scaled-polar optimality into a geometric condition on the positive polar factor of the gradient. For an arbitrary radial law, we obtained a complete characterization of this set as a translated and dilated spherical zonoid. The translation represents the isotropic baseline response, whereas the dilation contains all available nonscalar matrix freedom. The key quantity controlling this dilation is the atom–kink response capacity. It receives contributions only from radial atoms that align, after scaling, with nondifferentiable points of the curvature profile. Thus, nonscalar admissibility in the RR-ICM is not generated by radial concentration alone, but by an exact resonance between the radial law and the curvature kinks. This characterization yields a quantitative spectral-capacity bound and, in the atomless case, a sharp rigidity result: exact scaled-polar optimality can hold only when the positive polar factor of the gradient is scalar, or equivalently when the gradient is already a scaled column isometry. This rigidity highlights a singular feature of exact first-order optimality. A thin atomless shell may be arbitrarily close to a deterministic sphere, and the corresponding effective curvature profiles may be close in function value, while their admissibility geometries remain fundamentally different. The deterministic sphere can place all directional samples at the same kink and exploit the resulting interval of subgradients. An atomless radial perturbation hits each prescribed kink with probability zero and can therefore remove the entire direction-dependent slope-selection mechanism. Radial concentration does not, by itself, preserve the variational structure required for exact orthogonalization. This conclusion should not be interpreted as a limitation of Muon as an optimization method. Rather, it identifies a limitation of directional averaging as a curvature-based explanation of Muon’s polar update. The empirical effectiveness and established spectral interpretations of Muon suggest that its polar direction reflects a geometry more robust than the atom–kink mechanism available in the RR-ICM. Motivated by this tension, we introduced the Minimax RR-ICM, which retains the radial law, curvature profile, and directional state space of the RR-ICM, but replaces the prescribed uniform directional average by worst-case aggregation over probability laws on the sphere. We proved that, whenever a nonzero global minimizer exists, every such minimizer lies on the polar ray generated by the gradient. The radial law and curvature profile determine whether an optimizer exists and select its scalar magnitude, but they do not alter its normalized matrix direction. The scale is characterized by an exact one-dimensional convex problem involving the effective radial profile and the nuclear norm of the gradient. The Minimax RR-ICM therefore provides a new curvature-based minimax variational characterization of Muon’s polar direction. Importantly, the operator-norm geometry is not imposed through an external constraint, trust region, or norm budget. It emerges from robustifying the same radial-curvature model over directional probability laws. This supplies a direct variational bridge between the ICM viewpoint and existing spectral interpretations of Muon. The two models also admit a unified comparison through the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set. In the RR-ICM, admissible nonscalar spectra are confined to a translated and dilated spherical zonoid, whose size is governed by atom–kink resonance. In the Minimax RR-ICM, the admissibility set is instead a positive-semidefinite trace slab. The latter constrains the total spectral mass but accommodates every positive-semidefinite spectral shape with an admissible trace. Accordingly, the two models generate nonscalar freedom through different mechanisms: direction-dependent slope selection at radial atom–kink resonances in the RR-ICM, and the set-valued subdifferential geometry of the operator norm at a scaled polar point in the Minimax RR-ICM. Radial atomlessness destroys the former mechanism but leaves the latter matrix-shape freedom intact.

sections.heading: Scope and future directions.
sections.text: The present framework concerns exact optimality in a one-step curvature surrogate. It therefore does not by itself determine whether the radial fragility identified here leads to a substantial optimization error, nor does it describe the full training dynamics of practical Muon. The first natural direction is to develop a quantitative theory of approximate polar-factor admissibility. Although an atomless radial law eliminates the set-valued response required for exact scaled-polar optimality, a highly concentrated radial law may still make the polar update nearly optimal or place the true minimizer close to the polar ray. Relating the distance dist ⁡ ( S , A ⁡ ( J R , c ​ P ) ) \operatorname{dist}\bigl(S,A(J_{R},cP)\bigr) to an objective gap, a directional error, or the distance between the optimizer and the polar ray would determine whether radial fragility is only an exact first-order phenomenon or persists quantitatively. A second direction is to study directional ambiguity sets between the two endpoints considered in this paper. The RR-ICM fixes the uniform spherical law, whereas the Minimax RR-ICM optimizes over all probability laws on the sphere. Restricted ambiguity classes, such as divergence or transport neighborhoods of the uniform law, may generate intermediate Polar-Factor Admissibility Sets and interpolate between spherical-zonoid and positive-semidefinite trace-slab geometry. Characterizing this interpolation could quantify how much directional robustification is required to support a prescribed range of gradient spectra. More broadly, our results show that the variational geometry selected by an isotropic curvature model depends critically on how variation across perturbation directions is aggregated. Directional averaging makes exact polar optimality radially fragile, whereas full minimax aggregation makes the polar direction universal, conditional on the existence of a nonzero optimizer. The Polar-Factor Admissibility Set provides a common language for studying both endpoints and the geometries that may lie between them.

The Isotropic Curvature Model (ICM) provides a curvature-based explanation for this update by asking when gradient orthogonalization minimizes a one-step local-loss surrogate. We investigate the stability of this explanation when the fixed input radius of the ICM is replaced by a general radial law. We introduce the Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model (RR-ICM) and the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set, which encodes exact scaled-polar optimality as a geometric condition on the positive polar factor of the gradient. We derive an exact characterization of this set for arbitrary radial laws and show that all nonscalar admissible responses arise from radial atoms aligned with curvature kinks. Consequently, every atomless radial law exhibits zero-capacity rigidity: exact scaled-polar optimality is possible only when the gradient is already a scaled column isometry. To connect the curvature-based framework with the established spectral geometry of Muon, we introduce the Minimax RR-ICM by replacing directional averaging with worst-case optimization over probability laws on the sphere. We prove that every nonzero global minimizer lies on the polar ray of the gradient, while its scale is determined by a one-dimensional convex problem. The corresponding admissibility geometry is a positive-semidefinite trace slab, in sharp contrast to the spherical-zonoid geometry of the RR-ICM. Together, these results expose the radial fragility of average-curvature explanations and provide a new minimax variational characterization of Muon’s polar direction. 1 Introduction Muon is a matrix-aware optimizer designed primarily for hidden-layer weight matrices. Given a momentum-smoothed matrix gradient M t = U t ​ Σ t ​ V t ⊤ , M_{t}=U_{t}\Sigma_{t}V_{t}^{\top}, Muon applies a small number of Newton–Schulz iterations to approximate its polar factor U t ​ V t ⊤ U_{t}V_{t}^{\top} , while non-matrix parameters such as embeddings, normalization parameters, biases, and output heads are typically handled by AdamW [ 8 ] . Consequently, Muon preserves the left and right singular subspaces of the momentum update while largely flattening its nonzero singular values. In this sense, it replaces a potentially highly anisotropic matrix update by an approximately semi-orthogonal one. Muon first attracted attention through strong empirical performance in small-scale language-model and image-classification training, and was subsequently shown to scale to substantially larger language models. Liu et al. [ 14 ] identified weight decay and parameter-shape-dependent update scaling as key ingredients for stable large-scale training, and developed a memory- and communication-efficient distributed implementation. Their scaling-law experiments reported that Muon required approximately 52 % 52\% of the training FLOPs needed by a tuned AdamW baseline at matched performance. They further used Muon to train Moonlight, a 3 ​ B / 16 ​ B 3\mathrm{B}/16\mathrm{B} mixture-of-experts model, on 5.7 5.7 trillion tokens. These results suggest that matrix-gradient orthogonalization is not merely a small-model heuristic, but can provide meaningful optimization gains at the scale of modern language-model training. Earlier work on stochastic and preconditioned spectral descent already explored matrix updates adapted to spectral geometry [ 4 , 5 ] .
